strengths: Novel neuroscience-grounded approach that thoughtfully connects brain functional organization to modular architecture design
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation including routing analysis, ablations, neuroscience localizers, and steering demonstrations across multiple models
Well-designed baselines that effectively isolate the contribution of targeted specialization (General vs. Specialized experts)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates interpretable routing patterns and practical controllability through expert manipulation
Shows specialization persists through large-scale end-to-end training despite no explicit constraints
weaknesses: Performance improvements are modest and inconsistent (0.5-1.0 points across benchmarks), with some benchmarks showing degradation (e.g., MATH: 4.7→4.6 for LLAMA)
Critical finding that Specialized* (with irrelevant expert removed) often outperforms Specialized contradicts claims about specialization necessity—suggests removing experts can help rather than hurt
Theory of Mind expert fails validation with neuroscience localizers while language/MD succeed, significantly undermining the core neuroscience-grounding claim that experts align with brain networks
Reliance on GPT-4O pseudo-labels for Stage 1 training creates dependency on external large models, lacks quality validation, and offers limited guidance for domain adaptation
Evaluation limited to 1B parameter models with no evidence that benefits scale to larger models critical for modern LLMs
Complex three-stage training procedure plus curated dataset curation not justified by modest gains; no computational cost comparison provided
Many benchmarks require post-hoc GPT-4O clustering to demonstrate specialization; authors acknowledge many samples engage multiple domains, weakening specialization claims
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals provided; gains may fall within noise margins
Architectural components (parameter upcycling, MLP routing, top-1 routing) are established techniques; novelty primarily in curriculum and motivation
Test-time scaling analysis (Figure 12) shows performance degrades beyond top-2 routing, suggesting specialization benefits are limited and dilute with increased compute

strengths: Well-motivated interdisciplinary approach combining neuroscience and LLM design with clear cognitive domain background
Clever and data-efficient three-stage training curriculum that successfully induces and maintains specialization
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across seven benchmarks, two model architectures, and multiple test settings
Strong interpretability analysis with clear domain-aligned token routing patterns and layer-wise hierarchical organization
Unique controllability feature enabling steering of model behavior through expert ablation/activation
Robust reproducibility with extensive documentation, appendices, and methodological transparency
Demonstration that specialization persists through large-scale end-to-end training without explicit constraints
weaknesses: Modest and inconsistent performance gains (~1 point average) that don't justify architectural complexity; Specialized* variant often matches or exceeds Specialized, limiting evidence for specialization benefits
Incomplete brain alignment validation: Theory of Mind localizer fails to identify Social expert; only 2/3 localizers succeed, contradicting 'brain-like' framing in title and abstract

Critical unvalidated dependency on GPT-4O pseudo-labels with no inter-annotator agreement, label quality analysis, or sensitivity testing; labels may encode model biases rather than true cognitive domains
Limited scale: only 1B parameter models tested; unclear if specialization persists at larger scales (7B+), limiting relevance for 2025 venue standards
Weak baseline comparisons: General baseline uses random assignment; missing comparisons to ModuleFormer, other domain-specialized MoE, and non-brain-inspired modular approaches
Limited architectural novelty: core components (block cloning, MLP routing, top-1 routing) are standard; main novelty is training curriculum, not architecture
Steering behavior under-explored: only qualitative examples provided without systematic evaluation, automatic metrics, or user studies on output quality
Test-time scaling trade-offs (Figure 12) show performance degradation with top-3+ routing, contradicting specialization benefits narrative
Layer-wise hierarchical patterns could reflect general transformer properties rather than brain inspiration; alternative explanations not explored
Unvalidated dataset construction choices: 19 datasets arbitrarily selected, heavy O1 reliance for reasoning chains, imbalanced domain distribution

strengths: Novel and well-motivated brain-inspired modular architecture that grounds interpretability in neuroscience
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions: reasoning benchmarks, behavioral alignment (CogBench), neuroscience localizers, and systematic ablations
Strong interpretability results showing domain-specific token routing patterns that correlate with human judgments and recover known brain networks
Practical ability to steer model behavior at test time through selective expert activation
Rigorous experimental methodology with careful ablation studies demonstrating causal contributions of experts
Behavioral alignment is a meaningful contribution beyond standard performance metrics
weaknesses: Marginal and inconsistent performance gains on reasoning benchmarks that do not clearly justify architectural complexity; improvements often within noise without statistical significance testing
Critical scalability limitation: explicitly undemonstrated beyond 3B parameters, making applicability to modern LLMs (7B+, 70B+) unclear and severely limiting impact for 2024 submission

Insufficient ablations on key design choices: Stage 1 data necessity unclear (only 3,055 samples used), pseudo-labeling source (GPT-4o) not validated against alternatives, curriculum design (3 stages) not compared to alternatives
Potential circularity in evaluation: datasets selected for alignment with cognitive networks, then model is shown to learn that alignment; this is somewhat circular rather than true discovery
Limited experimental scope: only reasoning tasks evaluated; missing vision-language, diverse NLU tasks, and comparison to other mixture-of-experts or interpretability methods
Neuroscience claims need more careful framing: paper sometimes conflates 'inspired by neuroscience' with 'models neuroscience'; brain-to-expert mapping is not biologically precise or one-to-one
Incomplete statistical analysis: no significance testing across multiple benchmarks, inconsistent use of error bars, potential issues with multiple comparisons
Reproducibility concerns despite detailed appendices: reliance on closed-source models (GPT-4o, Llama) for core methodology; no code availability mentioned
